facts.statement: A seven-year-old boy named Diego Suárez discovered the first fossils of Chilesaurus on February 4, 2004.
facts.quote: Chilesaurus was first discovered on 4 February 2004 by a seven-year-old named Diego Suárez.

facts.statement: The initial discovery of Chilesaurus occurred while its discoverer and his geologist parents were searching for decorative stones in Chile's Aysén Region.
facts.quote: He and his parents, the geologists Manuel Suárez and Rita de la Cruz, were searching for decorative stones in the Aysén Region

facts.statement: The species Chilesaurus diegosuarezi was formally named and described in 2015 by a team led by Fernando Emilio Novas.
facts.quote: In 2015, the type species C. diegosuarezi was named and described by Fernando Emilio Novas, Leonardo Salgado, Manuel Suárez, Federico Lisandro Agnolín, Martín Dario Ezcurra, Nicolás Chimento, Rita de la Cruz, Marcelo Pablo Isasi, Alexander Omar Vargas, and David Rubilar-Rogers.

facts.statement: The genus name Chilesaurus combines the name of the country of discovery, Chile, with the Greek word for lizard.
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from Chile (the country where it was discovered) and the latinized Greek suffix "saurus", meaning "lizard".

facts.statement: The specific name diegosuarezi honors the seven-year-old boy who found the initial fossils.
facts.quote: The specific name honors Diego Suárez.

facts.statement: Chilesaurus lived approximately 148 to 147 million years ago during the Late Jurassic period in Chile.
facts.quote: Chilesaurus lived between 148-147 million years ago (Mya) in the Late Jurassic period of Chile.

facts.statement: Fossils of Chilesaurus were found at the Mallín Grande locality in the Chile Chico commune of the Aysén Region, Chile.
facts.quote: Sus fósiles fueron descubiertos en la localidad de Mallín Grande, comuna de Chile Chico, región de Aysén, en Chile.

facts.statement: Chilesaurus coexisted with small theropods, basal crocodilians, diplodocid and titanosaurian sauropods, and possibly brachiosaurids in the Toqui Formation.
facts.quote: Según los fósiles encontrados en la Formación Toqui, Chilesaurus coexistió con otro terópodo de tamaño pequeño, crocodiliformes basales, y dinosaurios saurópodos tanto diplodócidos como titanosaurianos y, posiblemente, brachiosáuridos.

facts.statement: The juvenile holotype specimen of Chilesaurus is estimated to have been about 1.6 meters long in life.
facts.quote: The holotype itself, which represents a skeletally immature individual, is estimated to have been about 1.6 m long in life.

facts.statement: Adult Chilesaurus is estimated to have reached a full length of about 3.2 meters.
facts.quote: The largest of these, believed to be an adult, was used to infer that the full length of an adult Chilesaurus would have been about 3.2 m.

facts.statement: Chilesaurus possesses unique skeletal features including a short premaxilla, a quadrilaterally-shaped coracoid, a hand with only two clawed fingers, and distinct hip and ankle structures.
facts.quote: It has a very short premaxillary bone, a uniquely quadrilaterally-shaped coracoid bone with thickened outer edges, a hand with only two clawed fingers (the third finger being highly reduced) with very shortened phalanges, and several features of the hip and ankle bones that are distinct from all other theropods.

facts.statement: Chilesaurus is distinguished by its unique spatula-shaped, elongated teeth that protrude forward from their sockets.
facts.quote: However, one of the most distinctive unusual features of Chilesaurus is its spatula-shaped, elongated teeth, which protrude forwards out of their sockets.

facts.statement: The unique tooth structure of Chilesaurus indicates it was a herbivore, a trait rare among theropods.
facts.quote: Such dentition would be unique among theropods, and is typical for a herbivore, indicating Chilesaurus was a plant-eater.

facts.statement: Chilesaurus has a backward-pointing pubic bone, interpreted as an adaptation for a complex digestive system required for herbivory.
facts.quote: Another apparent adaptation for herbivory is the backward-pointing pubic bone in the pelvis, which has been interpreted as an adaptation for developing the more complex digestive apparatus necessary to digest plants.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Chilesaurus may have used its strong arms and large first finger claw for defense.
facts.quote: However, it is possible that Chilesaurus could defend itself using relatively strong arms which bore a large claw on the first finger.

facts.statement: The classification of Chilesaurus is uncertain, with most researchers viewing it as a theropod and a minority suggesting it is an ornithischian.
facts.quote: While its exact classification is uncertain, many researchers believe it is a theropod, with a minority of academics suggesting that it may be an ornithischian.

facts.statement: Chilesaurus displays a mix of traits from theropods, ornithischians, and sauropodomorphs, challenging traditional dinosaur classification splits.
facts.quote: Showing a combination of traits from theropods, ornithischians, and sauropodomorphs, this genus has far-reaching implications for the evolution of dinosaurs, such as whether the traditional saurischian-ornithischian split is superior or inferior to the proposed group Ornithoscelida.

facts.statement: In 2017, Baron and Barrett proposed that Chilesaurus might be a basal member of the ornithischian group.
facts.quote: In 2017, Baron and Barrett proposed that Chilesaurus may instead be a basal ornithischian.

facts.statement: Despite subsequent studies, the classification of Chilesaurus remains uncertain as it has not been definitively tested as a theropod in all analyses.
facts.quote: However, Müller and colleagues also noted that Baron and Barrett did not test the original proposal of Chilesaurus as a theropod, and that its classification remained uncertain.

facts.statement: A 2024 study by Andrea Cau classified Chilesaurus as a sister taxon to the theropod clade Tetanurae.
facts.quote: In his major work on theropod classification in 2024, Andrea Cau recovered Chilesaurus as a sister taxon of Tetanurae.

facts.statement: A study by Fonseca and colleagues on ornithischian classification also recovered Chilesaurus as a theropod.
facts.quote: Fonseca and colleagues conducted a similar work on the classification of ornithischians, which also recovered Chilesaurus as a theropod.

facts.statement: If classified as a theropod, Chilesaurus would be one of very few non-coelurosaurian theropods to have evolved herbivory.
facts.quote: If Chilesaurus was a theropod, it would be only one of a handful of non-coelurosaurian theropods to evolve herbivory, alongside Limusaurus, Berthasaura, and possibly others.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Chilesaurus is a theropod or an ornithischian, though its theropod affinities are more widely supported by other researchers.
facts.quote: In a latter re-revision of his own datasets, Baron concluded that Chilesaurus remains enigmatic and could be either a theropod or an ornithischian, while noting that its affinities as a theropod were more generally supported by other authors.

facts.statement: Chilesaurus measured approximately 3.2 meters from nose to tail.
facts.quote: Chilesaurus medía unos 3,2 metros de la nariz a la cola.

facts.statement: Its small head featured small, spatulate teeth pointing obliquely forward, a unique trait among theropods.
facts.quote: La pequeña cabeza tiene dientes pequeños, en forma de espátula apuntando oblicuamente hacia delante.

facts.statement: An adaptation for eating plants included a pubic bone in the pelvis that pointed backward.
facts.quote: Otra adaptación para comer plantas, es que el hueso púbico en la pelvis apunta hacia atrás.

facts.statement: Its hind limbs were less adapted for running, indicated by a small cnemial crest on the front upper part of the tibia and a wide foot with a weight-bearing first toe.
facts.quote: Los miembros posteriores de Chilesaurus se habían vuelto menos adaptados a correr, como se muestra por una pequeña cresta cnemial en la parte superior frontal de la tibia, y un amplio pie, con un primer dedo de soporte del peso.

facts.statement: It could defend itself with a robust arm equipped with two claws, the first being large and very extended, similar to basal sauropodomorphs.
facts.quote: Chilesaurus podría defenderse con un brazo robusto, provisto de dos garras, la primera grande y muy extendida, al igual que los sauropodomorfos basales.

facts.statement: The first fossils of Chilesaurus, a vertebra and a rib, were discovered on February 4, 2004, in Mallín Grande, Chile Chico commune, by seven-year-old Diego Suárez while accompanying his geologist parents.
facts.quote: Los primeros fósiles de Chilesaurus, una vértebra y una costilla, se descubrieron el 4 de febrero de 2004 en la localidad de Mallín Grande, comuna de Chile Chico, por el —en ese entonces— niño de siete años Diego Suárez, que acompañaba a sus padres, los geólogos Manuel Suárez y Rita de la Cruz.

facts.statement: The type species Chilesaurus diegosuarezi was named and described in 2015 by Argentine paleontologist Fernando Novas and his collaborators.
facts.quote: En 2015, la especie tipo, Chilesaurus diegosuarezi, fue nombrada y descrita por el paleontólogo argentino Fernando Novas y sus colaboradores.

facts.statement: The holotype SNGM-1935 was found in a layer of the Toqui Formation dating to the late Tithonian.
facts.quote: El holotipo, SNGM-1935, se encontró en una capa de la Formación Toqui, que data de finales del Titoniense.

facts.statement: The holotype consists of a fairly complete and articulated juvenile skeleton with a skull, but lacking the feet and most of the tail.
facts.quote: El holotipo, SNGM-1935, se encontró en una capa de la Formación Toqui, que data de finales del Titoniense. Se compone de un esqueleto de un individuo juvenil bastante completo y articulado, con el cráneo, pero que carece de los pies y la mayoría de la cola.

facts.statement: Chilesaurus lived during the Tithonian stage, from 149.2 to 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Tithonian to Tithonian (149.2 to 143.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: Chilesaurus was originally placed in a basal position within the Tetanurae clade among theropods.
facts.quote: Chilesaurus fue ubicado originalmente en una posición basal del clado Tetanurae, entre los terópodos.

facts.statement: This genus shows a confusing mix of traits normally present in ceratosaurians, basal sauropodomorphs, and ornithischians.
facts.quote: Este género muestra una confusa mezcla de rasgos normalmente presente en celurosaurios, sauropodomorfos basales y ornitisquios.

facts.statement: An alternative classification proposed by Baron and Barrett in 2017 suggests Chilesaurus could be a basal ornithischian, with ornithischians being closer to theropods than to sauropodomorphs, forming a group called Ornithoscelida.
facts.quote: Una clasificación alternativa propuesta por Baron y Barrett en 2017 indica que Chilesaurus podría ser un ornitisquio basal, y los ornitisquios a su vez serían más cercanos a los terópodos que a los sauropodomorfos, formando un grupo conocido como Ornithoscelida.

facts.statement: However, Müller et al. noted that Baron & Barrett did not prove the original proposal of Chilesaurus as a theropod, and that its classification remained uncertain.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, Müller et al. también señalaron que Baron & Barrett no probó la propuesta original de Chilesaurus como terópodo, y que su clasificación aún era incierta.

facts.statement: Chilesaurus is classified under the parent group Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Parent group: Ornithischia

facts.statement: New specimens discovered in 2008 were initially thought to belong to several different dinosaur species, but were later found to belong to the same species with a strange combination of traits.
facts.quote: En 2008 se descubrieron nuevos especímenes, pero se creyó que pertenecían a varias especies de dinosaurio diferentes. Solo más tarde fue cuando se dieron cuenta de que pertenecían a la misma especie con una extraña combinación de rasgos.

rejected.statement: Chilesaurus had hind limbs less adapted for running, evidenced by a small cnemial crest on the shinbone and a broad foot with a weight-bearing first toe.
rejected.quote: The hind limb of Chilesaurus is less adapted for running than many other groups of dinosaurs. This is inferred from the presence of a small cnemial crest on the front top of the shinbone, and a broad foot with a weight-bearing first toe.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'shinbone and a broad foot with a weight-bearing'
